column3: Its divided handling of a shared affair is the closest lexical and structural parallel to the focus's internal rupture.
A group gathers to settle its affair while plotting, adding a parallel of collective decision-making concealed from the observer.
It establishes that private speech and counsel remain heard and recorded, extending the focus's hidden consultation beyond its apparent privacy.
It repeats the division of a shared affair into parties, but adds less than the earlier, nearer formulation in 21:93.
Pharaoh's proposed appointment begins the staged contest whose participants later fracture into private counsel.
The raised couches do not clarify the contest's dispute or its concealed consultation.
It presents people disputing a matter among themselves before acting, a broader decision-making parallel already supplied more directly above.
Musa's warning is the immediate speech that precipitates the magicians' dispute and secret counsel.
The exposure of secrets adds the prospect that concealed motives behind the counsel can become manifest.
It closely parallels the concealment of group counsel and adds the public relabeling of truth as magic.
It states that both inward secrecy and private counsel are known, reinforcing the non-absolute privacy of the focus scene.
It shows internal dispute over a shared matter producing failure and disobedience, clarifying the destabilizing force of such division.
Concealed regret after judgment gives a later consequence of hidden inner response, but not the focus's deliberative scene.
The agreed public time and assembly complete the immediate setting in which the private dispute occurs.
It directly links mutual dispute to weakness and loss of collective force, supplying a clear consequence of the focus's division.
It joins secret and open speech under complete knowledge, a useful but already well-established secrecy parallel.
Pharaoh's gathering of his scheme immediately precedes the warning and the magicians' internal consultation.
It makes every private consultation present to divine knowledge, extending the focus's hidden gathering without its contest context.
Concealed regret is distant from the focus's active, collective deliberation.
It parallels the later accusation that a messenger's truth is deceptive magic and threatens inherited practice.
Its contrast route and scene of facing couches do not add positive evidence for the concealed dispute.
Whispering among people is present, but its eschatological setting and content do not clarify the magicians' consultation.
The next ayah discloses the substance of the private counsel: casting Musa and Harun as magicians who threaten the established way.
The equivalence of hidden and open speech is a generic secrecy statement already covered by stronger cards.
The consequence of a prior affair does not illuminate the focus's dispute or counsel.
It shows the counselors moving from disagreement and concealment to a unified instruction to consolidate their scheme.
The couch reference is a contrast route without relevance to the focus's action.
It characterizes harmful private talk as an instrument for distress, giving a moral-function parallel to secret counsel.
It follows the hidden consultation with the assertion that all speech is known, supporting the scene's limited secrecy.
A concealed agreement to obey opposition shows private coordination becoming an outward course of action.
The oath by those who pull out does not clarify dispute or confidential counsel.
Dismissive hearing of a revealed reminder only broadly precedes the secret counter-speech in its local passage.
Divine knowledge of what is hidden and announced adds only the generic secrecy point already established.
Nuh's request for judgment and rescue does not develop the focus's collective consultation.
It condemns fabrication against God and denial of signs, supplying a warning-framework for the false framing at issue in the contest.
Private and public address occur together, but this missionary pattern does not clarify the group's secret resolve.
The rule against choosing otherwise after divine decision does not address the magicians' internal deliberation.
Turning away and waiting provides only a distant parallel of withholding engagement.
Hidden calculations becoming regret are only a remote consequence parallel.
It depicts forbidden private counsel organizing sin, aggression, and disobedience, a close functional parallel to covert hostile coordination.
The rejection of revealed warning as manifest magic directly parallels the counsels' characterization of Musa.
Private and public giving does not clarify the focus's secret meeting.
Removal of rancor among companions in Paradise is not a relevant counterpart to hostile counsel.
Successive dismissive labels for a messenger's message reinforce the relabeling pattern already seen in the focus's aftermath.
A prohibition on disputing the messenger in a matter is only a broad normative contrast to the focus.
The description of the Fire does not illuminate the consultation.
The demand to alter recitation and the response of authorized revelation extend the counterfeit-versus-authorized-message issue.
Rules for private marriage proposals do not clarify the collective hostile counsel.
The eating scene has no bearing on the focus.
Divine knowledge of hidden and open matters is redundant generic background for secrecy.
Mutual consultation over a shared affair supplies a constructive counterpart to the focus's divided and covert deliberation.
A group withdraws for private consultation after public options fail, closely paralleling a confidential decision space without the same conflict.
The punishment garment scene does not clarify the focus.
Musa's being brought near for private speech gives a distinct, positive form of confidential address involving the same prophet.
An unsuccessful scheme against Ibrahim only broadly parallels plotting against a prophet.
Knowledge of secrets supports a general background point but adds no scene-level parallel.
Guidance and restoration do not clarify the secret counsel.
It links anticipated mutual dispute over an affair with failure, but repeats a consequence already shown more directly in 3:152 and 8:46.
The effacing of stars does not bear on the focus.
Hidden communication directed to an opposing side shows secrecy functioning as a channel of disloyal coordination.
The punishment scene does not explain the focus's counsel.
Listeners form private counsel to reduce a messenger to a discrediting label, closely matching the disclosed aim of 20:63.
The abundance of corruption is too general to clarify the focus.
It distinguishes forbidden private counsel from counsel for goodness and piety, giving a normative boundary for the focus's secret talk.
The settling of an affair and sincerity do not specifically illuminate internal dispute or private counsel.
Private delight within one's family does not add to the focus.
Division into factions supplies a broader counterpart to the focus's internal fragmentation, though without its counsel scene.
The exchange of a cup is unrelated to dispute over an affair.
The punishment for prior disbelievers does not clarify the focus's deliberation.
Yusuf's inwardly withheld response is individual restraint, not the collective secret counsel at issue.
Listening to falsehood and judging between parties lacks a specific link to the focus's private dispute.
Private speech with the messenger concerns regulated access rather than collective hostile planning.
The rescue and punishment of Shuayb's people do not clarify the focus.
A confidential report becomes disclosed through divine knowledge, adding a transmission-and-exposure counterpart to secret speech.
The command to guard one's family from the Fire has no focused connection.
Joyful return to family does not clarify the focus.
A party turns away from divine judgment, only broadly resonating with resistance to a messenger.
Knowledge of hidden and open speech is another generic, redundant secrecy statement.
Yaqub's inward need does not concern the group consultation or dispute.
Protection and joy on the final day do not add to the focus.
Enmity and hatred placed among a community give a distant consequence of internal division.
The rescue of Salih and believers does not clarify the focus.
Its private-conference regulation repeats the counsel setting without bearing on the focus's dispute or plot.
Disagreement among recipients of knowledge through mutual transgression supplies a broad parallel of internal division after truth arrives.
It directs disputants to return their contested matter to God and the Messenger, a normative counterpoint to the focus's private handling.
It connects human disagreement with prophetic sending and a Book for judgment, framing the resolution of contested matters after clear proofs.
Musa's later rescue offers narrative continuation but does not explain the consultation itself.
Reconciliation between parties is only a general counterpart to dispute.
Mutual religious denials illustrate factional dispute, but add little after the stronger division cards.
The rescue of Hud and believers does not clarify the focus.
The rescue of the faithful is too remote from the focus's internal counsel.
Judgment among all by truth is a distant final counterpart to disputing parties.
Recording expenditure and travel does not bear on the focus.
Mercy among believers provides only a broad opposite to the focus's internal contention.
Household eating permissions do not clarify the focus.
Divine governance of the cosmic affair does not illuminate the group's disputed affair.
The legal punishment instruction is unrelated to the focus.
The orphan reference has no connection to the focus.
Testimony procedures do not clarify the focus's secret counsel.
Ibrahim's request for reassurance and its sign do not bear on the focus.
The immediate declaration that God knows the secret and what is still more hidden directly frames the concealed counsel in this passage.
Pharaoh's charge that Musa seeks to expel them through magic establishes the contest accusation later repeated within the counselors' speech.
The magicians' request that Musa or they begin shows the public action that follows their hidden deliberation and consolidated scheme.
A group leaves public assent to devise by night a contrary plan, closely paralleling concealed collective opposition after a public encounter.
It explicitly depicts people hiding their night-time planning from others though not from God, a direct counterpart to secret hostile counsel.
It gives a governing distinction among private counsels by their content, supplying a direct evaluative frame for the focus's najwa.
Pharaoh's chiefs identify Musa as a knowledgeable magician, an alternate narrative presentation of the accusation disclosed after the focus.
The claim that Musa seeks to expel them from their land supplies the same threatened-order rationale voiced by the counselors in 20:63.
The chiefs' collective advice to defer Musa and mobilize gatherers shows deliberation becoming an organized response.
The order to bring every skilled magician completes the counsel's conversion into a coordinated contest strategy.
The chiefs of Pharaoh's people press a policy response to Musa, extending the contest into elite collective opposition.
The coordinated plotting to restrain, kill, or expel a messenger is a close functional parallel to hostile counsel becoming a collective plan.
The labeling of arriving truth as manifest magic is a direct accusation-pattern parallel to the focus's disclosed counsel.
The appeal to inherited ways and fear of altered authority closely parallels the counselors' concern for their established path.
Pharaoh's command to bring every learned magician shows the official consolidation of the response discussed in the focus sequence.
The brothers jointly propose alternatives against Yusuf, providing a clear example of group deliberation directed toward a harmful plan.
A counterproposal within the brothers' discussion makes internal disagreement part of the formation of their shared scheme.
Their agreement on Yusuf's placement shows deliberation reaching coordinated execution, comparable to the focus's next movement in 20:64.
Pharaoh presents Musa to the chiefs as a knowledgeable magician, a close alternate rendering of the focus's accusation.
The threatened expulsion and appeal for the chiefs' judgment reproduce the political rationale and collective deliberation of 20:63.
The chiefs answer with a strategy to defer the opponents and send mobilizers, showing counsel taking operative form.
The gathering of skilled magicians extends the coordinated response but adds less than the preceding deliberative instruction.
The magicians' assembly at an appointed time realizes the public mobilization decided through the counsel.
The queen's refusal to decide an affair without her council supplies a constructive counterpart to group deliberation over a shared matter.
The council's collective response shows reciprocal consultation before a ruler's decision, though without secrecy or hostility.
The queen's assessment of kings' destructive entry informs the stakes that can shape counsel over political threat.
Her choice to send a gift tests the situation before committing to a course, adding deliberation through strategic restraint.
A group plans a night plot against a messenger, closely paralleling hidden counsel serving coordinated hostile action.
The chiefs are explicitly consulting to kill Musa, a particularly close instance of elite secret deliberation against the same prophet.
The settling of an affair is answered by divine counter-determination, extending the focus's disputed affair into the question of whose plan prevails.
